title: SQL Stored Procedures and SQLite Alternatives
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose and behaviour of SQL Stored Procedures and SQLite Alternatives.
Write SQLite-compatible SQL for the topic or a clearly labelled equivalent.
Predict result rows using the lesson's sample data.
Identify dialect limitations, NULL behaviour and common errors.
Apply the topic to a practical data task.

understand.concept: A stored procedure is a named routine stored in a database and invoked to perform a sequence of operations. Procedure syntax, parameters, variables and invocation commands vary by DBMS. SQLite has no native CREATE PROCEDURE or CALL statement, so SQL Playground cannot execute stored procedures.
understand.whyItMatters: Stored procedures can centralize repeatable business operations, enforce consistent workflows and reduce duplicated SQL. Learners must also know when a database engine does not provide this feature.
understand.analogy: Think of a SQL query as a carefully specified instruction for selecting or shaping rows in a database.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not model SQL evaluation order, transaction guarantees, NULL logic or DBMS-specific implementation details.

explain.narrative:
## Stored procedure concept
A procedure is a database routine that can accept parameters and execute one or more statements. MySQL commonly uses CREATE PROCEDURE ... BEGIN ... END and CALL; SQL Server uses CREATE PROCEDURE and EXEC; PostgreSQL supports procedures with CALL and also functions. These syntaxes are not interchangeable.

## MySQL-style illustration (not executable in SQLite)
```sql
DELIMITER //
CREATE PROCEDURE GetOrdersForCustomer(IN p_customer_id INT)
BEGIN
  SELECT order_id, amount
  FROM orders
  WHERE customer_id = p_customer_id;
END //
DELIMITER ;
CALL GetOrdersForCustomer(7);
```

SQLite deliberately has no stored-procedure language. The examples below run in SQLite and demonstrate adjacent database techniques—views, transactions, triggers and temporary tables. They are alternatives or building blocks, not stored procedures. In an application, reusable parameterized SQL can be prepared and invoked by application code.

## Common mistakes
- Assuming syntax is identical across all database engines.
- Omitting explicit column lists when moving data.
- Ignoring NULL, constraints or result ordering.
- Treating a documented dialect example as executable SQLite syntax.

## Best practices
Use explicit columns, test against the target DBMS/version, keep setup scripts repeatable, and verify results with SELECT queries.

examples.title: Use a view for a reusable query
examples.explanation: A view stores a reusable query definition, but it is not a parameterized stored procedure.

examples.title: Group multiple statements in a transaction
examples.explanation: A transaction groups statements atomically; it does not create a callable database routine.

examples.title: Use a trigger for automatic database-side work
examples.explanation: A trigger runs automatically after a matching event; it is different from a procedure explicitly called by a client.

examples.title: Use a temporary table for a multi-step workflow
examples.explanation: A temporary table can hold intermediate results for a connection-local workflow.

examples.title: Keep reusable reporting logic in a view
examples.explanation: A view can centralize reporting logic; application code still supplies filters and parameters.

practise.guidedTask: Run the five examples in order. Before each run, predict the result and explain how SQL Stored Procedures and SQLite Alternatives affects it.
practise.independentTask: Create your own small dataset and write three new queries using SQL Stored Procedures and SQLite Alternatives. Include one boundary case and document the expected output.
hints: Read the target DBMS syntax notes before running an example.
Use explicit column names and aliases where they improve clarity.
Check NULL values separately from zero and empty strings.
Use ORDER BY when the display order matters.
Compare the returned rows with your prediction after execution.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes SQLite stored procedure support?
options: SQLite has no native CREATE PROCEDURE or CALL statement
SQLite supports MySQL DELIMITER syntax
SQLite procedures are created with CREATE ROUTINE
SQLite automatically converts views into procedures
questions.answer: SQLite has no native CREATE PROCEDURE or CALL statement
questions.explanation: Stored procedures are not a native SQLite feature; the other DBMS examples must not be run in SQLite.

questions.prompt: Which practice is safest for this topic?
options: Name columns explicitly and verify dialect support
Assume all SQL dialects use identical syntax
Ignore NULL and constraint behaviour
Rely on implicit row order
questions.answer: Name columns explicitly and verify dialect support
questions.explanation: Explicit columns, dialect checks and clear assumptions make SQL predictable.

questions.prompt: What should a learner check before relying on this feature?
options: The target DBMS and its supported syntax
Only the browser screen size
The name of the SQL file
Whether the query has uppercase keywords
questions.answer: The target DBMS and its supported syntax
questions.explanation: SQL syntax and behaviour can vary between database engines and versions.

questions.prompt: Which statement about query results is correct?
options: A result should be ordered explicitly when order matters
Rows are always returned in insertion order
Aliases change the stored source table
Comments alter the result set
questions.answer: A result should be ordered explicitly when order matters
questions.explanation: Without ORDER BY, SQL does not guarantee a particular result order.

questions.prompt: How should this topic be practised in the CodeSaathi SQLite Playground?
options: Run the provided SQLite-compatible examples and distinguish documented dialect syntax
Paste unsupported DBMS syntax and assume it will run
Skip the setup statements
Treat expected output as a database command
questions.answer: Run the provided SQLite-compatible examples and distinguish documented dialect syntax
questions.explanation: The Playground runs SQLite, so dialect-specific syntax must be labelled and translated to a supported equivalent.
